Printed parts for the cube solver

Two designs: the six-motor frame for the finished robot, and the one-motor bench stand for the first test. Blue parts are the prints. Drag to rotate, scroll or pinch to zoom.

Six-motor frame

Modelled on the layout in your photo: the bottom motor hangs under a raised deck, four side motors sit on towers around the cube, and the top motor rides on a plate that lifts off. The corners stay open so two cameras can each see three faces.

Show
View

Motors and cube are stand-in blocks at their datasheet sizes. I checked the model for collisions: no printed part touches a motor, another printed part, or the space the cube's layers sweep as they turn, including with the towers pushed fully in.

PartPrintSize as printedHow it prints
Base: deck on four legs1200 × 200 × 61 mmUpside down, deck on the bed. No supports.
Tower for a side motor442 × 76 × 108 mmStanding on its foot. No supports.
Top plate1140 × 140 × 10 mmUpside down, flat face on the bed. No supports.
Shaft adapter618 × 18 × 28.5 mmSame adapter as the bench stand. Tip still a placeholder.
  • What the motors sit on: each motor is held by four M3 screws through its front face, which is how NEMA 17 motors are made to mount. Each side motor also rests in a cradle on its tower: a shelf under the body and a cheek on either side. The top motor stands on the top plate. The bottom motor hangs from the deck by its four screws.
  • FabLab fit: the base is the largest part at 200 mm square. It fits the Prusa (250 × 210 mm bed) and the PolyPrinter (229 mm). Everything is five separate prints, so each is a short job.
  • Material: about 670 cm³ of solid volume across all parts. At normal infill I estimate 290 to 330 g of PLA, about $15 to $17 at the FabLab's rate. That is a rough figure.
  • Hardware: 24 M3 × 10 mm screws for the six motors, 8 M3 × 12 mm screws with nuts to bolt the towers to the deck, and 8 M3 × 16 mm screws to hold the top plate to the towers.
  • Loading the cube: lift the top plate off, slide the towers back along their slots, drop the cube onto the bottom adapter, then push the towers in and refit the top. This is slow for every solve; a quicker latch can come once the adapter tip is settled.
  • Same spacing as the bench stand: every motor face is 32 mm from its cube face, so one adapter design serves both.
  • Not yet designed: camera mounts, lighting, and a tray for the driver boards.

One-motor bench stand

It bolts to one stepper motor and cradles the cube so the motor turns a single face while the other two layers stay still.

The 3D view needs WebGL, which this browser has turned off. The dimensions and notes below describe the same part.

The motor and cube are simple stand-in blocks at their catalogue sizes, not models of the real parts. "Turn the face" plays a quarter turn in slow motion so you can see the corners clear the base.

Were the real parts measured?

Not with calipers, but every motor and cube dimension now comes from the documents for the exact parts you ordered. The motor numbers are from the 17HE19-2004S datasheet drawing, and the cube size is from TheCubicle's listing. One thing is still a guess: the square recess under the cube's centre cap, which no one publishes.

The stand can be printed as it is. Datasheet numbers have tolerances and printers shrink parts slightly, so the cube may sit a little loose or snug in the cradle; the 0.6 mm clearance is one number to change if the first print is off.

How the adapter reaches the cube

  • It is used, and it is a separate small print. The grey sleeve in the view slides over the motor shaft, is locked onto the shaft's flat with one M3 screw, and ends in a square tip that sits in the recess under the cube's centre cap.
  • One fix since the first version. The shaft is fully round for its first 9 mm and only has a flat on the last 15 mm. The first adapter had a flat-sided hole all the way down, which would have jammed on the round section. The hole is now round where the shaft is round.
  • The tip needs your measurement. When the cube arrives, pop off one centre cap and measure the recess width, its depth, and how far the screw head stands up. Those three numbers replace the placeholders.

The FabLab takes STL files, you run the printer yourself after staff training, and prints must be collected within 14 days.
